items.title: Decide how Fixed::FromString() should read "12.5%" and oversized numbers
items.details:
`base/fixed.cc`.

- "12.5%" reads as 12%, since the percentage takes only the leading digits; the original read it as the decimal 12.5, because it counted a `%` only right after the digits. A whole part past INT_MAX reads as 0, while smaller ones keep their low byte.
- Parsing once into a decimal (int64 digits over 10^k, at most eight fraction digits) and scaling to 8.8 once would read "12.5%" as 12.5% and wrap every oversized value alike. No shipped rules value changes; found by the `/simplify` stage of the `base/fixed` `/modernize-file` run (`4e995aa2..8fd12531`).
items.author: agent
items.toDecide:
How should `Fixed::FromString()` read a fraction before `%` and a whole part that does not fit?

- **Keep**: "12.5%" is 12%, a whole part past INT_MAX is 0 and smaller ones keep their low byte. Nothing to do.
- **Parse once into a decimal and scale once**: "12.5%" becomes 12.5% and every oversized value wraps alike; about 30 lines plus tests. No shipped rules value changes.

after: // Empty text, and any part with no digits, reads as zero.

items.title: Check that Red Alert's scenario INI numbers team and trigger types the same way both ways
items.details: The writers emit a type's position in its heap's in-use list (`PositionOf()`), the readers resolve the number as a slot index (`SlotOrNull()`): `ra/ai/tevent.cc` (~651 write, ~674 read), `ra/ai/trigger_action.cc` (~161, ~174), `ra/ai/team_type.cc` (`TeamType::ToIniEntry()` writes the trigger's position, `ReadIniEntry()` reads a slot, in both scenario formats). They agree only while the type heaps have no holes, which holds after a fresh INI load; a type deleted in the scenario editor leaves one. The original game had the same pairing. Either write `SlotIndexOf()` or check that the editor saves its types in slot order.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: The pairing is right as it stands: types are written in in-use-list order, so `PositionOf()` is the place of the entry, which is the slot the type gets when the scenario is read into empty heaps; `SlotIndexOf()` would break after a deletion. `ReferencesSurviveWritingAndReadingHeapsWithHoles` pins that. The one real mismatch was on the read side: `TeamType::ReadIni()` freed a rejected entry at once, moving every later team type down a slot; it now frees the rejects after all entries are read (`ReadIniLeavesTheSlotOfARejectedEntryEmpty`).

items.title: Decide whether Tiberian Dawn's Target::Make() should mask its value to 12 bits
items.details:
- `Make()` (was `Build_Target()`) ORs the whole value over the kind (`td/core/target.h`), so a cell of -1 becomes the word 0xFFFF: kind 15, which names nothing, yet true as a bool. A team mission `TMISSION_MOVE` or `TMISSION_UNLOAD` whose waypoint is unset (`init.cc` fills the waypoints with -1) sends its units to that word (`td/ai/team.cc`, `TeamClass::AI()`), as does a `TMISSION_MOVECELL` argument outside 0..4095; the original did the same.
- Masking would turn -1 into cell 4095 and change play, so it needs its own commit and an xcheck reference update.
items.author: agent
items.toDecide:
- **Keep**: a cell of -1 makes the word 0xFFFF (kind 15, which names nothing, yet true as a bool), as the original did.
- **Mask the value to 12 bits**: -1 becomes cell 4095, so a team whose waypoint is unset heads there. Changes play; its own commit and an xcheck reference update.

items.title: Decide which RTTI_CELL encoding Red Alert's cell targets should use
items.details:

- A mismatch the original already had: the construction yard's ARCHIVE event sends `FromCellIndex(cell)` (`ra/objects/building.cc`, `Active_Click_With()`), and the MCV it undeploys into is sent to that word with `Assign_Destination()`, which reads it as a sub-cell spot, so it heads for the wrong cell.

items.title: Send both games' PLACE event through its own constructor
items.details:
- `DisplayClass::Mouse_Left_Release()` (`ra/map/display.cc`, `td/map/display.cc`) passes `cell.index() + ZoneOffset`, an `int`, so the event is built by `EventClass(type, RTTIType, int id)`, which fills `Data.Specific.ID`; the PLACE handler reads `Data.Place.Cell`, the low half of that int on a little-endian machine. items.title: Check whether a captured object leaves stale threat in the houses' regions
items.details:
- An object adds its `Risk()` to the other houses' `Region`s on `MARK_DOWN` and subtracts it on `MARK_UP` (`ra/objects/object.cc:1668,1682`, via `CellClass::Adjust_Threat()` in `ra/objects/cell.cc:1710`), and each call reads `Owner()` and the alliances afresh. `TechnoClass::Captured()` (`ra/objects/techno.cc:4047`) changes the owner without lifting the object, so the later `MARK_UP` skips the new owner and subtracts from the old one, which never had the amount added: the new owner keeps the threat for good and the old owner's region goes negative. items.title: Fix the source sampling in ScaleRotateShape(), then step the coordinates incrementally
items.details:
`ra/assets/shape_draw.cc`.

The destination-to-source mapping has three defects, visible on an 8x6 test shape at a half turn, at west, and at north with scale 0x180:

- It maps each destination pixel's corner (`x - width`), not its centre, so the result sits one pixel off the centre of the doubled frame.
- `static_cast<int>` truncates toward zero, so source coordinates in (-1, 1) all become 0: the first source row and column are drawn one pixel too wide (13 columns where 12 are right at scale 1.5).
- At quarter turns `std::cos`/`std::sin` return about 1e-16 instead of 0, so coordinates that should be exact integers fall on either side of a pixel boundary and rows come out spliced or duplicated.

Fix: sample the pixel centre (`x + 0.5 - width`, `y + 0.5 - height`), take `floor`, and use exact matrix entries (0, +-1) when the angle is a multiple of 64. Expected results: a half turn of an 8x6 shape is the source reversed in columns 4..11, rows 3..8; north at scale 1.5 is 12x9 in columns 2..13, rows 1..9 with every source pixel 1 or 2 wide. Add golden unit tests for these (the function has none); it changes how every rotated or scaled shape draws, usually by a one-pixel shift, so re-record the `tools/ui_check.py` screenshots that change.

Then step the source coordinates per x (start computed once per row, a constant added per pixel) instead of four multiplies per pixel. Measured 2026-10-05 on the current mapping: 11.3 -> 8.0 us per 48x48 shape, but 5,503 of 10,240 rotation/scale/size cases moved pixels, 90% of them at quarter turns, because the accumulated rounding crosses the same exact boundaries. With centre sampling only 175 cases differ (odd-sized shapes at quarter turns, where a half-pixel centre still lands on a boundary); keep the stepping only if the golden tests and a sweep of all 256 rotations show it reproduces the corrected output exactly, e.g. by using the exact integer path for quarter turns. `std::floor` is a libm call without SSE4.1 and cost more than the stepping saved (30 vs 11 us), so floor with integer arithmetic or an offset that keeps the value positive.

items.title: Finish what the ra/ai/special_options modernization left
items.details:
Follow-up to `2d3c8713..820577e9`. Done 2026-10-05 in two commits, one per game; decisions taken interactively with the user.

**Decisions**

1. `three_point_turns`: the check box is gone from RA's dialog; the bit stays.
2. The unread flags (`ore_grows`, `ore_spreads`, `three_point_turns`) and their writers stay: no save or wire change.
3. Escape cancels in both games. RA already did (only its header comment was stale); TD's dialog now does too.
4. Names: `SpecialFlags` / `TheSpecialFlags()`, `shadow_grows`, `AskDifficulty()`, in both games where they apply.
5. The flag struct lives in `<game>/core/special_flags.h`.
6. `Reset()` (RA) and `Init()` (TD) are gone; the owner in `startup/game.h` starts from the flags' defaults.
7. The one-shot `redraw` flag stays.

**What changed**

- RA: `ra/ai/special_options.*` split into `ra/core/special_flags.h` (the struct), `ra/screens/special_options.{h,cc}` (`RunSpecialOptionsDialog()`, now one check box, speed build, on the first row) and `ra/screens/difficulty.{h,cc}` (`DifficultyChoice`, `DifficultyForLevel()`, `AskDifficulty()`). Tests split the same way; new ctest target `ra_difficulty_test`.
- TD: `td/ai/special.*` became `td/core/special_flags.h` (`SpecialClass` → struct `SpecialFlags`, `TheSpecial()` → `TheSpecialFlags()`, all 29 `Is...` members renamed to snake_case, e.g. `IsRoad` → `no_road_pieces`, `IsBarOn` → `all_health_bars`, `IsHealthBar` → `enemy_health_bars`) and `td/screens/special_options.{h,cc}` (`Special_Dialog()` → `RunSpecialOptionsDialog()`, rewritten around a constexpr table of label + get/set per flag; no `Setting` mirror, no label switch). New `td/screens/special_options_test.cc` (six scripted tests, target `td_special_options_test`).
- Deviation from decision 6: the initializer is `SpecialFlags special_ = InitialSpecialFlags();`, a constexpr function in each `special_flags.h`, not `{.ore_grows = true, .ore_spreads = true}`. The designated form fails the strict build twice over: `-Wmissing-designated-field-initializers` wants every flag named and `readability-implicit-bool-conversion` rejects `true` for an `unsigned` bit-field.
- The flags stay `unsigned x : 1` with no default member initializers (raw in `EventClass`'s union and the packets).

**Verified**

Full strict build clean; 1,612 ctests pass in `build` and `build-strict`; `tools/net_check.py` in step for 600 frames; `tools/ui_check.py` all 12 scripts ok after re-recording `src/ra/testdata/ui/special_options` (two shots changed because the three-point box is gone; the script's click moved from row two to row one).

**Left open**

- Not checked by hand: TD's dialog on a real display, and a TD multiplayer game (there is no TD net check). TD's wire layout is unchanged (same bit order), only names moved.
- `ra/core/special_flags_test.cc`: CLion's "unused local" on the RAII `Installed<>::Scope` is a false positive, as in `ra/saveload/saveglobals_test.cc`.

items.title: Check the unguarded waypoint index in TeamClass::Is_Leaving_Map
items.details:
A review during the team type run (`30c6f6ae..e9ac6245`) reported, and nobody has yet confirmed, that `TeamClass::Is_Leaving_Map()` (`ra/ai/team.cc`, the anchor) indexes `TheScenario().Waypoint` with a script line's argument without the `static_cast<unsigned>(value) < kWaypointCount` test that the other uses in `team.cc` (~698, ~717, ~2967) have. Confirm with a test that builds such a team and calls `Is_Leaving_Map()`; if it aborts, add the same range test (a few lines). Not a change for a well-formed scenario.

items.title: Name the two rules for what counts as a waypoint
items.details:
Red Alert tests a waypoint number against two limits without saying which is meant. Below `ScenarioClass::kHomeWaypoint` (98) is "a waypoint the designer names by letters": the team editor's mission argument (`ra/editor/team_type_dialog.cc`, the anchor), `ra/editor/mapedit.cc` ~961 and ~979, `ra/objects/cell.cc` ~1073. items.title: Decide whether the computer should pick among more than twenty team types
items.details:
`TeamType::SuggestNewTeam()` (`ra/ai/team_type.cc`, the anchor) collects candidates into a fixed array of 20 in heap order and draws one at random, so in a scenario with more than 20 eligible team types for a house the later ones are never created by the house's own AI. `TheTwentyFirstCandidateIsNeverOffered` in `ra/ai/team_type_test.cc` pins it.

To decide: it is the shipped behaviour. Lifting the cap (a `std::vector`, 5 lines) changes which team a house builds and what the synchronized random stream returns afterwards, so missions with many team types play differently and a multiplayer game against an unchanged peer desyncs. Run `30c6f6ae..e9ac6245`.

- **Lift it** (a `std::vector`, 5 lines): changes which team a house builds and what the synchronized random stream returns afterwards, so missions with many team types play differently and a game against an unchanged peer desyncs.

items.title: Silence the nullability-extension warnings the strict build prints for Abseil's CHECK macros
items.details:
The strict (clang, `-Weverything`) compile prints `warning: type nullability specifier '_Nullable' / '_Nonnull' is a Clang extension [-Wnullability-extension]` for every `CHECK_EQ` / `CHECK_GE` / `CHECK_LT`-style macro in project code; the note points at `absl_nullable` in `absl/base/nullability.h`. They are warnings, not errors, so the build passes, but each recompiled unit adds dozens of lines that bury real output. Seen on recompiling `engine/crypto/pk.cc`: 36 from `engine/crypto/digit_cursor.h`, 16 from `engine/stream/byte_stream.h`, 8 from `engine/crypto/int.h`, 6 from `game/core/object_heap.h`. 28 files under `src/` use these macros.

`.clang-tidy` already turns the same diagnostic off for the clang-tidy pass (`-clang-diagnostic-nullability-extension`, line 64); the compiler flags do not. Add `-Wno-nullability-extension` to the Clang `add_compile_options` list at the anchor, with a comment naming Abseil's macros. One line; it changes every strict compile command, so the next strict build recompiles the tree (ccache misses) and clang-tidy re-runs only where its own command changes.

items.title: Decide whether Direction256Toward should stop landing one step short
items.details: `Direction256Toward()` (was `Desired_Facing256()`) returns `DirType::kEast - 1` for a target due east, `kSouth - 1` due south, `kSouthEast - 1` on the exact south-east diagonal and `kNorthWest - 1` on the exact north-west one; north, west, north-east and south-west are exact. The cause is the `- 1` in `fraction = 0x40 - fraction - 1` in `src/game/sim/direction.cc`, which is right for every non-exact angle (it makes that half of the quadrant round the same way as the other) and wrong only when `smaller * 32 / bigger` divides exactly. `direction_test.cc` pins the current results (`EastAndSouthLandOneStepShort`, `TwoDiagonalsLandOneStepShort`), and `src/ra/core/coord_test.cc` notes it too.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `Direction256Toward()` now rounds the ratio up in the half of a quadrant that counts back from its end axis (`0x40 - ceil(smaller * 32 / bigger)`) instead of subtracting one from the rounded-down ratio, so all eight compass directions are exact; every other exactly dividing ratio in that half (for example 1 in 2) moves one step too. The pinning tests in `direction_test.cc` and `ra/core/coord_test.cc` expect the exact values, and the hashes of four UI scripts whose in-mission screenshots shifted were re-recorded.
items.toDecide:
This is the shipped behaviour of both games and runs inside the simulation (aiming, turret and aircraft facing, scrolling).

- **Leave it**: nothing changes; the tests already document it.
- **Fix it** (subtract the 1 only when the division leaves a remainder): units aim one step (1.4 degrees) differently on the four exact angles, a fixed build desyncs against an unfixed peer, and recordings and the save/load smoke tests can diverge.

decisions.question: Should Direction256Toward stop landing one step short on due east, due south and the exact south-east and north-west diagonals?

items.title: Decide whether FacingSector was meant to round like NearestFacing
items.details: `FacingSector()` (was `Dir_To_8()`) in `src/game/sim/direction.h` truncates a direction to the facing below it. The original read `(dir | 0x10) / 32`; the OR set a bit the division dropped, so it did nothing and this run removed it. The original author probably meant the `+ 0x10` that `NearestFacing()` has. items.title: Find why the coverage build's test discovery hit a bus error
items.details: The first `tools/coverage.py --tests game_sim src/game/sim/direction.h src/game/sim/direction.cc` of this run failed while linking: `gtest_discover_tests` ran `build-coverage/src/engine/window/engine_window_test` and got `Result: Bus error`, which stopped the build. Running the same executable by hand a moment later worked, and the second `tools/coverage.py` run passed. The coverage build links with `-fprofile-continuous`, which maps the profile file into memory, so a likely cause is two executables (or discovery and another job) sharing one profile path under the parallel build. Check what `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` is during discovery and give each executable its own pattern (`%p` or `%m`), or have `tools/coverage.py` retry.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Cause: `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` was unset during the build, so every test executable that `gtest_discover_tests` ran wrote `./default.profraw` in its binary directory; under `-fprofile-continuous` two executables of one directory (`engine_window_test` and `engine_window_keyboard_test`) mapped the same file and one truncating it killed the other with SIGBUS. Reproduced by running the two with `--gtest_list_tests` concurrently: 14 of 300 rounds died with exit 135, 0 of 300 with separate profile files. `tools/coverage.py` now runs the build with `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<build-dir>/discovery-profiles/%c%m.profraw` (new `profile_env()`, shared with `run_test`), so each binary has its own file.

TD code still names the slots directly: `mapeddlg.cc` draws the "Rock/Wall/Road" and "Neutral Unit" legend with `game::kBrown` and `game::kPurple`; `findpath.cc`'s debug overlay uses `game::kCyan` (313), `game::kBrown` (1147, 1612) and `game::kLightBlue` (441, 527, 1621); `score.cc` (1871, 1874) and the "raised blue" box colors in `ui/dialog.cc` (133-134) use `game::kLightBlue`. Replace those with the `kCc...` aliases so the name matches what shows on screen. No behaviour change. Check with `git grep -nE 'game::k(Purple|Cyan|Brown|LightBlue)' -- src/td`: only the four alias definitions should remain.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Replaced the 12 direct uses of `game::kPurple`/`kCyan`/`kBrown`/`kLightBlue` in `mapeddlg.cc`, `findpath.cc`, `score.cc` and `ui/dialog.cc` with `kCcOrange`/`kCcBlueGreen`/`kCcTan`/`kCcBlueGrey`. items.details: What the `/modernize-file` run on `src/engine/gfx/pcx_file.{h,cc}` found and left: the PCX reader still lives in each game, Red Alert has its own writer, and a few clean-ups reach outside the two files.

items.title: Move the PCX reader into the engine beside the writer
items.details:
`Read_PCX_File()` and its `BufferedFileReader` are defined twice, in `src/td/startup/nondosstub.cc` (declared in `td/startup/winstub.h`) and in `src/ra/startup/nondosstub.cc` (declared in `ra/assets/filepcx.h`), while the writer is `engine::gfx::WritePcxFile()` in `src/engine/gfx/pcx_file.cc`. The reader belongs there too: it needs only `PixelBuffer`, `Palette` and `OpenGameFile()`, all of which `engine_gfx` may include.

- Move TD's copy to `engine/gfx/pcx_file.{h,cc}` as `engine::gfx::ReadPcxFile()`, convert its Westwood banner, and move the reader tests from `src/td/assets/pcx_test.cc` to `src/engine/gfx/pcx_file_test.cc` (they can then round-trip with the writer).
- Diff RA's copy against TD's before deleting it; both callers are `Load_Title_Screen()`.
- The `backing`/`size` parameters are passed as `{}` and `0` by every caller found; check and drop them.

The run did not make the move because it crosses from the games into an engine library.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: The reader is `engine::gfx::ReadPcx(ByteStream&)` and `ReadPcxFile(file_name)` in `engine/gfx/pcx_file`, returning an optional `PcxPicture` (size, pixels, palette); both games' copies, `ra/assets/filepcx.h` and `td/assets/pcx_test.cc` are gone and the tests live in `pcx_file_test.cc`. The stream-or-name question was answered as for the writer (T-196): both. Found on the way and fixed in `640a4097`: a picture cut short read the palette as pixels.
items.toDecide: Go ahead with moving `Read_PCX_File()` out of both games into `engine/gfx/pcx_file`? And should it keep taking a file name, or read from a `ByteStream&` the caller opened (see the writer's item)? About 80 lines per game, 6-8 files.

decisions.question: Go ahead with moving `Read_PCX_File()` out of both games into `engine/gfx/pcx_file`?
decisions.answer: move Read_PCX_File to the engine too, but do it as part of /modernize-file, otherwise the code will look ugly

items.title: Decide whether WritePcxFile takes a stream or a file name
items.details:
`engine::gfx::WritePcxFile(std::string_view file_name, PixelView&, const Palette&)` opens the file itself with `OpenGameFile(name, FileAccess::kWrite)`. Red Alert's own writer, `ra::Write_PCX_File(ByteStream&, PixelBuffer&, const Palette&)` in `src/ra/assets/writepcx.cc`, takes a stream its caller opened (RA's callers pick `OpenDiskFile`).

With a `ByteStream&`: the engine function loses the open and two includes, its tests write to a memory stream instead of a temporary file, and RA's four callers become drop-in. Cost: TD's five callers (`td/debug/debug.cc`, `td/map/gscreen.cc`, `td/ui/screenshot.cc`, `td/startup/scripted_run.cc`, `td/assets/pcx_test.cc`) each gain an `if (const auto file = Open...)`; about 7 files, 30 lines. A caller that opens the file first leaves an empty file behind when the view cannot be locked, where today no file is created.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Added `engine::gfx::WritePcx(ByteStream&, PixelView&, const Palette&)`, which does the work and reports short writes; `WritePcxFile(name, ...)` stays as a wrapper that encodes first and then opens with `OpenGameFile`, so a view without pixels still creates no file and TD's callers are unchanged. The tests write to a recording stream, with three file tests left for the wrapper.
items.toDecide: `ByteStream&` (RA's shape, caller opens the file), keep the file name, or the stream form plus a small name-taking overload?

decisions.question: What should engine::gfx's PCX writer take: a stream, a file name, or both?

items.title: Replace Red Alert's own PCX writer with the engine's
items.details:
`src/ra/assets/writepcx.cc` and `src/ra/assets/filepcx.h` hold a second `Write_PCX_File()`, `Write_Pcx_ScanLine()`, `PCX_HEADER` and `RGB`, duplicating `engine::gfx::WritePcxFile()`. Callers: `ra/startup/conquer.cc:620`, `ra/startup/scripted_run.cc:45`, `ra/ui/screenshot.cc:41`, `ra/screens/credits_roll_test.cc:60`.

The two encoders differ: RA caps a run at 47 pixels (`rle_max_run = 0x2F`) where the engine's uses the format's 63, and RA writes the picture's size into the header's resolution fields where the engine writes 320x200. Both read back the same, but the file bytes change, so re-record anything that hashes RA's PCX output (`tools/ui_check.py --accept` after checking the pictures).

Deleting RA's copy also removes its latent stride defect (separate item).
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Deleted `ra/assets/writepcx.cc` and its test, plus `PCX_HEADER`, `RGB` and `Write_PCX_File()` from `filepcx.h`; the four callers call `engine::gfx::WritePcx()` on the stream they opened and `Read_PCX_File()` reads `engine::gfx::PcxHeader`. The ten RA `ui_check` hash files are re-recorded: all 47 screenshots decode to the same pixels and palette as before, only the file bytes differ.

items.title: Fix the row stride and missing lock in Red Alert's Write_PCX_File
items.details:
`ra::Write_PCX_File()` steps through `pic.view().pixels()` by `pic.width() + pic.view().x_add()`, which leaves out the buffer's `pitch()`, and never locks the view: for a surface-backed `PixelBuffer` the rows are skewed, and while the surface is unlocked `pixels()` is empty and the first `subspan` runs past its end. Every caller passes a memory buffer, so it is latent.

The engine's writer had the same defect, fixed in `f588fbad` (lock the view, use `stride()`); `engine/gfx/pcx_file_test.cc`'s `WritesASurfaceSkippingItsRowPadding` is the test to copy. Goes away by itself if RA switches to the engine's writer.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `ra::Write_PCX_File()` now locks the buffer's view for the duration (writing nothing if it will not lock) and steps rows by `stride()`. New `ra_writepcx_test` (`src/ra/assets/writepcx_test.cc`) covers a memory buffer, a padded surface and a surface that refuses to lock; the surface test crashes against the old code.

items.title: Hide PcxHeader in pcx_file.cc once the reader is in the engine
items.details: `engine::gfx::PcxHeader` is public in `src/engine/gfx/pcx_file.h` only because Tiberian Dawn's `Read_PCX_File()` reads through it, and the header's magic values (10, 5, 1, 8, 1) are written in `pcx_file.cc` and checked again by hand in `td/startup/nondosstub.cc`. When the reader moves into `pcx_file.cc`, move the struct into its anonymous namespace, name the magic values once, and take the sentence about TD out of the struct's comment.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Moved `PcxHeader` into the anonymous namespace of `pcx_file.cc` (and dropped `<array>` from the header). `pcx_file_test.cc` now builds its input headers by named byte offset (`HeaderOf()` returns the 128 bytes, `SetField()` stores a 16-bit field). The magic values were already named once (`kPcxId` ...) and TD's hand check and the TD sentence went with T-195.

comments.author: agent
comments.text: Unblocked by T-195, but `pcx_file_test.cc` now builds its input files from `PcxHeader` (`HeaderOf()`), besides taking its size. Hiding the struct means the test writes the header by byte offset, as `WritesTheHeaderOfAnEightBitPicture` already does for the expected bytes.

// 16-bit fields are little-endian and all fall on even offsets, so the struct

items.title: Decide whether a PCX scanline is padded to an even length
items.details: `WritePcxFile()` sets the header's `bytes_per_line` to the picture's width. The PCX specification requires an even number, so a picture of odd width is written with an odd one. The games' own reader accepts any value not below the width; a strict third-party reader may not. Padding means writing one extra byte per row for odd widths, which changes the file bytes (and any recorded screenshot hash of an odd-width picture).
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `WritePcx()` now writes an even `bytes_per_line` (`BytesPerLine()`): a row of odd width ends in a repeat of its last pixel, which `ReadPcx()` already drops. The widest writable picture is 32766 pixels instead of 32767; even-width pictures, which is every screenshot the games take, are written byte for byte as before.
items.toDecide: Pad odd-width scanlines to an even `bytes_per_line` as the specification says, or leave the files as the original game wrote them?

decisions.question: T-200: should WritePcx() pad an odd-width scanline to an even bytes_per_line, as the PCX specification requires?
options: Leave as the game wrote them

anchors.text: int BytesPerLine(const int width) { return width + (width % 2); }
before: // Returns the bytes a scanline of a picture `width` pixels wide decodes to.
// The format wants an even number, so a row of odd width is one byte longer
after: // Appends `pixels`, one row of the picture, to `encoded` as a run-length
// encoded PCX scanline, padded to BytesPerLine().

items.title: Decide what resolution a written PCX header states
items.details: `WritePcxFile()` writes 320 and 200 into the header's `horizontal_dpi` and `vertical_dpi` whatever the picture's size, as the Tiberian Dawn original did; Red Alert's own writer puts the picture's width and height there. Readers ignore the fields, so this only matters for agreeing on one writer.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Decided to keep 320x200. Both games already share the one writer, so no code changed; the comment in `WriteEncoded()` now says why the value stays (no reader uses it, and the `tools/ui_check.py` hashes cover the header bytes).
items.toDecide: Keep 320x200, write the picture's size as Red Alert does, or write a real dpi?

decisions.question: What should a written PCX header state in horizontal_dpi / vertical_dpi?

items.title: Reject a picture too large for a PCX header
items.details: `WritePcxFile()` narrows `view.width() - 1`, `view.height() - 1` and the width into the header's `int16_t` fields with `static_cast`. A view wider or taller than 32768 pixels writes a header that does not describe the scanlines after it. No screen is that large; return false before opening the file (with a test) rather than write a corrupt picture.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `LockedScanlines()` now asks `FitsHeader(view)` first, so `WritePcx()` and `WritePcxFile()` return false and write nothing (no file is created) for a view wider than 32767 or taller than 32768 pixels. Four tests cover the largest size that is still written and the rejection of a wider and a taller one, through the stream and the file.

items.title: Check the result of WritePcxFile in Tiberian Dawn's screenshot code
items.details: `engine::gfx::WritePcxFile()` returns whether the picture was written since `99201dd4`; it used to return 0 on every path. None of the four callers looks: `td/ui/screenshot.cc:34`, `td/debug/debug.cc:148`, `td/map/gscreen.cc:436`, `td/startup/scripted_run.cc:38`. At least the scripted run (`-SCRIPT`, used by `tools/ui_check.py`) should report a shot it could not save on stderr; the function could also be `[[nodiscard]]` once they do.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: All four callers check the result: the scripted run prints `-SCRIPT: cannot write <path>` on stderr, the screenshot key, the debug key and the screen recorder `DLOG(WARNING)`. `WritePcxFile()` is `[[nodiscard]]`. Red Alert's `WritePcx()` callers are T-219.

items.title: Add a scoped lock for PixelView
items.details:
`PixelView::Lock()` / `Unlock()` are paired by hand at about 35 sites, with the rule that `Unlock()` must not follow a failed `Lock()`; an early return between them leaks a nested lock count. Nothing in `src/base`, `src/engine` or `src/game` wraps the pair (`ra::LockedWindow` in `ra/assets/winbits.cc` is tied to the window table).

Add a small guard to `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.h`, for example `class PixelLock { explicit PixelLock(PixelView&); explicit operator bool() const; ~PixelLock(); }`, non-copyable, unlocking only if it locked, with tests in `pixel_buffer_test.cc` (about 20 lines each). First users: `WritePcxFile()` in `engine/gfx/pcx_file.cc`, `engine/gfx/wsa_animation.cc` and `ra::LockedWindow`; the other sites are an optional sweep.

items.title: Which other code can be migrated to Rust
items.author: user
items.resolution: Surveyed `src/engine`, `src/base` and `src/game` against what made LCW a good first kernel (pure bytes-in/bytes-out, no engine types in the signature, few callers, existing tests). The ranked candidates are in the comment; no code changed, and no migration was started because which one to do is the user's call.

comments.author: agent
comments.text:
## Survey (2026-10-09)

Criteria, from the LCW migration (`docs/RUST_LCW_PLAN.md`): a leaf function over byte/int slices, no engine classes in its signature, a handful of callers, tests that can run old against new, and ideally a hot inner loop where the C++ bounds checks cost something. Line counts are the `.cc` without tests.

### Tier 1: same shape as LCW, drop-in behind the existing C++ signature

| Code | Lines | Callers | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `engine/codec/xor_delta.cc` (`ApplyXorDelta`, `ApplyXorDeltaToView`) | 135 | `gfx/keyframe.cc`, `gfx/wsa_animation.cc` | Format 40 delta; always runs right after an LCW decode, so both halves of a shape/WSA frame decode would be Rust. Smallest step. |
| `engine/codec/aud_decoder.cc` (`DecodeAdpcmBlock`, `DecodeWestwoodBlock`) + `engine/video/vqa/adpcm_decoders.cc` | 132 + 74 | audio mixer, VQA loader | IMA ADPCM and Westwood 8-bit; state is one small POD (`AdpcmState`) that maps to a cxx shared struct. |
| `engine/video/vqa/vq_decoder.cc` (`DecodeVqFrame`) | 85 | `movie_drawer.cc` only | Codebook block copy per movie frame; with LCW it is the whole VQA video path. |
| `engine/crypto/sha1_compress.cc` | 226 | `sha.cc` only | Portable + SHA-NI paths; Rust has `is_x86_feature_detected!` and the same intrinsics. `SHAEngine` stays C++. |
| `engine/crypto/blowfish.cc` | 656 (mostly tables) | pk sink/source, MIX, RA saves | Needs an opaque Rust type (`Box<Blowfish>`) behind `BlowfishEngine`, or a key-schedule struct C++ owns. |
| `engine/codec/lzw.cc` | 290 | `compressed_block.cc` only | Self-contained engine with internal tables; low value (only LZW12/14 blocks use it). |
| `engine/codec/base64.cc` | 445 | INI, WOL, tools | Easy, cold. |
| `engine/crypto/key_phrase_hash.cc`, `base/random.cc` | 117, 105 | few | Trivial; `RandomClass` must stay bit-identical for multiplayer sync and is cheaper left alone. |

### Tier 2: worth it, larger

- `engine/crypto/mp.cc` (3,014 lines) + `pk.cc` (389): the RSA-style bignum. Only user is `int.h`/`pk.cc`, the interface is digit slices, and it was 24% of Debug load CPU. The biggest single win in unsafe-pointer-arithmetic removed, but it is 60-odd `XMP_*` functions; the sane cut is to move the whole `PKey` encrypt/decrypt behind 2-3 bridge functions and delete `mp.cc`, not bridge each `XMP_*`.
- `third_party/lzo` (711 lines, `lzo1x_c/d`): used by RA save games through `block_backends.cc`. Must stay byte-compatible on decode; encode only has to round-trip. A pure-Rust LZO1X crate could replace the vendored C.
- `engine/gfx/fading_table.cc` (79): pure palette math, 15% of Debug load CPU; needs the 256-entry palette passed as a `&[u8]` rather than `Palette`.
- `engine/gfx/shape_blitter.cc` (258) and the `BlitToLocked`/`ScaleLocked`/glyph loops in `pixel_buffer.cc`: hot per-frame pixel loops, but the signatures take `PixelView`; migrating means first splitting each into a clip step in C++ and a slice+stride kernel.
- Format parsers on a byte span: `gfx/pcx_file.cc` (319), `gfx/cps_image.cc`, `gfx/ico_image.cc`, MIX header parsing in `file/mix_archive.cc`, and a `cargo fuzz` target comes almost free for each.

### Not worth migrating

- `engine/stream` and the sink/source adapters, `engine/file` (GameFile, SearchPaths, `ini_file.cc` with 77 includers), `engine/net`, `engine/window`, `engine/audio/audio_mixer.cc`: virtual C++ interfaces, SDL or sockets, or wide caller fan-out. cxx would bridge every call and nothing gets simpler.
- `game/`, `ra/`, `td/`: the object hierarchy is virtual inheritance with pooled raw pointers and globals; no boundary to cut at.
- `base/fixed.h`, `base/strings`: header-level vocabulary inlined into 64+ TUs; an FFI call per operation would be slower.

### Suggested order

1. `xor_delta` (finishes the shape/WSA decode path, a day at most).
2. `aud_decoder` + `adpcm_decoders` + `vq_decoder` (finishes the VQA/audio decode path; frame-dump and golden tests already exist).
3. `sha1_compress` and `blowfish` (the MIX-open path, with `mix_archive_test` as the guard).
4. `mp.cc`/`pk.cc` as its own plan.

items.title: Decide whether Link's add functions unlink a node that is still in a list
items.details: `Link::InsertAfter()`, `AppendTo()` and `PrependTo()` overwrite the node's `next_`/`previous_` without unlinking it. A node that is still linked elsewhere leaves its old neighbours pointing at it: the old list is cut short or closed into a ring (the ring guards in `HeadOf()`/`TailOf()` in `link.h` exist only for this; `link_test.cc`'s two ring tests show it). Commit 60609cee made only the three already-in-place cases no-ops. No caller was found doing this; the dialogs call `ForgetNeighbors()` (was `Zap()`) on every gadget before rebuilding a list.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `InsertAfter()`, `AppendTo()` and `PrependTo()` now `DCHECK` that the node is in no list (after the already-in-place early returns); the ring guards stay because the normal `NDEBUG` build still lets it through. A sweep of the gtests and `tools/ui_check.py` in a build with DCHECKs on found three callers, all fixed: `ListClass`/`TListClass` unlink their scroll gadgets before re-adding them (`UnlinkScrollGadgets()`), and `SliderClass` no longer chains its ± buttons behind itself in the constructor, which every dialog's `AppendTo()` cut off again.
items.toDecide:
Should the three add functions call `Link::Remove()` on the node first?

- **Yes**: adding a linked node moves it cleanly, and the ring guards in `HeadOf()`/`TailOf()` can go. Risk: after `ForgetNeighbors()` a node's old neighbours still point at it, so a later `Remove()` on such a neighbour writes through stale pointers into a list that has already been rebuilt. Needs the ~150 `ForgetNeighbors()` callers looked at (see the sibling item) and a UI check of the sidebar and the network dialogs.
- **No, CHECK instead**: `DCHECK(next_ == nullptr && previous_ == nullptr)` in the three functions finds a misusing caller in debug runs; small.
- **Leave it**: documented in the class comment as it is now.

items.title: Replace Link::ForgetNeighbors() with something that cannot leave stale pointers
items.details: `ForgetNeighbors()` (the legacy `Zap()`) clears a node's two pointers and leaves the neighbours pointing at it. It was written for nodes whose pointers started out uninitialized; they are initialized to nullptr now. About 150 callers in both games (sidebar, `netdlg.cc`, `wol_gsup.cc`, `wolapiob.cc`, `mapeddlg.cc`) call it on every gadget of a list before rebuilding the list, which only works when none is missed: a missed gadget keeps pointers to nodes that are now in another list, or destroyed. Options: replace each call by `Remove()` (safe one node at a time, O(n) walk each); or give the list head one function that unlinks the whole chain and call that once per rebuild. Either changes how UI lists are torn down, so check with `tools/ui_check.py` and a network lobby.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Every gadget list is a `game::GadgetList` over a vector (`docs/GADGET_LIST_PLAN.md`, commits 4f1ad716..cfc8a308); `Clear()` empties one and keeps the focus. `Link` and `ForgetNeighbors()` are deleted.

items.title: Decide which one-pixel-too-large fills are bugs
items.details:
The sweep that gave `PixelView::FillRect` / `DrawRect` a `Rect` kept every call's pixels. 128 calls now read `Rect::FromCorners(...)`; many of them are `FromCorners(x, y, x + w, y + h)`, the legacy inclusive-corner call written without the `- 1`, so the box is one pixel wider and taller than `w` x `h`. Find them with `grep -rn "Rect::FromCorners" src`. Examples:

- `src/td/ui/dialog.cc`: `Draw_Box` fills and outlines `x + w`, `y + h`.
- `src/td/editor/mapedit.cc`: `Rect{0, 0, 641, 17}` on a 640 pixel wide view (was `FillRect(0, 0, 640, 16)`).
- `src/td/screens/ending.cc`: `Rect{0, 360, 639, 39}` stops at column 638 and leaves column 639.
- `src/td/screens/mapsel.cc` and `src/td/screens/score.cc`: the text-erase fills, and the casualty bars `FromCorners(0, y, min(i, killed), y + 1)` that draw one column for a count of 0.
- `src/ra/editor/mapedtm.cc`, `src/ra/editor/mapedplc.cc`, `src/ra/map/help.cc` (`DrawX + Width + 1`).

Related change of behaviour to know about: the old `FillRect` swapped its corners, so a width of 0 drew a two-pixel column; `Rect{x, y, 0, h}` draws nothing. No `ui_check` screenshot changed.

items.title: Decide whether PKey should encode keys longer than 512 bits in full
items.details:
`PKey::Encode_Modulus()` and `PKey::Encode_Exponent()` (`src/engine/crypto/pk.h`) write only the low 64 bytes of a 2048-bit number: `der_encode()` in `src/rust/src/pk/mod.rs` searches for the top byte from byte 63, not 255. A modulus of more than 512 bits (two primes above 256 bits) comes out cut short, and decoding it back gives a different key.

The behavior is inherited on purpose. The C++ `XMP_Encode()` (now `src/engine/crypto/mp_reference_test_util.cc`) started its scan at the register's length in 32-bit digits instead of in bytes, and the Rust port keeps it so that `pk_differential_test` can compare encodings byte for byte. The cargo test `der_encode_sees_only_the_low_512_bits` pins it.

Nothing in the games calls the two functions; only the tests and `kernel_bench` do, to copy a key between the two implementations. The games' MIX key is 319 bits.

A fix is small: scan all `NUMBER_BYTES`, use the long form of the DER length above 127 bytes, raise `MAX_DER_BYTES` and `PKey::kMaxEncodedBytes` (67) to 261, and restrict the differential test's encoding comparison to numbers of at most 512 bits, where the reference is right.
items.author: agent
items.toDecide:
Fix the encoder so that it writes the whole number, or keep it identical to the C++ one?

- **Fix:** about an hour. Keys of up to 2048 bits round-trip through `Encode_*`/`Decode_*`; the differential test can no longer compare encodings above 512 bits with the reference.
- **Keep:** nothing to do now; it becomes free to fix once the C++ reference is deleted (see the item about removing the reference kernels).

after: /// The number of bits in `number` up to and including the highest one set.

items.title: Fix the division by zero for a public key with no usable modulus
items.details:
`PKey::Block_Count()` (`src/engine/crypto/pk.h`) divides by `Plain_Block_Size()`, which is 0 for a key whose modulus is zero or has fewer than 10 bits: a default-constructed `PKey`, or the one `IniFile::GetPublicKey()` returns when the INI has no usable `[PublicKey]` section, since malformed DER leaves the modulus as it was.

`MakePkDecryptSource()` (`src/engine/crypto/pk_source.cc:40`) and `MakePkEncryptSink()` (`src/engine/crypto/pk_sink.cc:48`) call it unconditionally, so opening an encrypted MIX archive with such a key is an integer division by zero (SIGFPE on x86), not a failed open.

The formula is the original one; the C++ `PKey` before the Rust migration behaved the same. Found by reading, not reproduced.

Fix: have both factories return `nullptr` when `key.Plain_Block_Size() <= 0` (the decrypt one already returns `nullptr` for a short header, and `MixArchive::Open()` handles it), and make `Block_Count()` return 0 for such a key instead of dividing. Add a test to `pk_stream_test.cc` with a default `PKey`, and one to `mix_archive_test.cc` that an encrypted archive opened with a default key fails to open.

items.toDecide:
Keep the shipped look, or pass 4 so frames 0-2 are shown?

- Keep: nothing to do; close as wont_fix.
- Pass 4 with the same rates: the door takes 30 frames to open instead of 10 (3 instead of 1 for the fast case), which delays unloading - a simulation change, so multiplayer against an unfixed peer desyncs.

items.title: Decide whether the two games' StageCounter should become one game::StageCounter
items.details: `ra::StageCounter` and `td::StageCounter` have the same interface. They differ in the countdown: Red Alert's is an `engine::platform::Timer<game::FrameTickSource>`, so it keeps time in frames where `AI()` is not called; Tiberian Dawn's is a `uint8_t` decremented per `AI()` call, with a `uint16_t` stage, and those widths are the save layout. TD's narrow fields carry two latent defects: `SetRate()` keeps the low byte (a rate of 256 would stop the animation; every caller passes less), and `AI()` with a rate but a countdown of 0 (a damaged save only) wraps to 255 calls. Red Alert has `IsAboutToChange()`, TD does not.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Merged on the frame clock, as decided: RA's class is now `game::StageCounter` in `src/game/sim/stage_counter.h` and TD uses it. TD `kSaveGameVersion` 12 with a new fixture; six TD UI script hashes re-recorded (animation timing shifts by up to a frame per `SetRate()`).
items.toDecide:
Merge them into `src/game/sim/stage_counter.h`, or leave one per game?

- Merge on the frame-clock timer: TD's stage then advances by game frames, not by `AI()` calls. That is a simulation change wherever TD skips `AI()` for an object, and a `kSaveGameVersion` bump for TD with a new fixture; check with `tools/td_saveload_smoke.sh`.
- Merge as a template over the countdown: exact, but keeps both mechanisms.
- Leave them: nothing to do; the latent defects could still be closed by widening TD's fields to `int32_t` (save bump only).

items.title: Keep two Red Alert team or trigger types of the same name from corrupting a saved scenario
items.details: `TeamType::WriteIni()` and `TriggerType::WriteIni()` store each type with `ini.PutString(section, IniName, ...)`, which replaces an entry of the same name. Two types with one name therefore leave a single entry, while the references in the file are still numbered by position in the in-use list (`PositionOf()`), so every reference to a type after the lost one reads back one slot off, and the lost type is gone. Nothing in the editor checks for a taken name: `trigger_type_dialog.cc` (~1384) names every trigger type left blank `____`, so two unnamed ones already collide. Either refuse a taken name in the team and trigger dialogs, or make the writers fail loudly on a duplicate. Seen while fixing T-32.

items.details: T-191 dumped the palette files: TD's TEMPERAT, DESERT and WINTER palettes hold the same sixteen colors in slots 0-15 as Red Alert's. items.title: Move the clipping functions into namespace base and pass them a Rect
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `OutCode`, `OutCodeOf()`, `ClipRect()` and `ConfineRect()` are in `namespace base`. `ClipRect()` takes a `base::Rect` and returns what is left (the default `Rect` when nothing is, so callers ask `IsValid()`); `ConfineRect()` takes a `base::Rect` and returns a `base::ConfinedRect` (`position`, `bounded`). The 11 call sites in `engine/gfx` and both games' `map/display.cc` and `map/radar.cc` are converted, and the dead re-clamp after `ConfineRect()` in `Scroll_Map()` is removed.

items.title: Clip the fill and the stamp with ClipRect() instead of their own intersections
items.details:
Two drawing functions still intersect a rectangle with a window by hand, which is what `base::ClipRect()` (`src/base/clip.h`) does:

- `PixelView::FillRectLocked` in `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.cc` computes `x1`/`y1`/`x2`/`y2` with `std::max`/`std::min` and its own empty test. Replace with `base::ClipRect(rect, width_, height_)` and `IsValid()`.
- The tile draw in `src/engine/gfx/stamp.cc` intersects the tile with a clip window that is not at the origin. Clip the tile rectangle with `ClipRect()` while it is still relative to the clip corner, then add `clip_x`/`clip_y`.

No behaviour change; `engine_gfx_test` covers both.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `PixelView::FillRectLocked` and `PixelView::DrawStampLocked` now clip with `base::ClipRect()` and test `IsValid()` instead of computing their own intersections. The stamp clips the tile while it is still relative to the clip corner and adds `clip_x`/`clip_y` only for the destination offset.

items.title: Pass ConfineRect() the window as a Rect so callers stop translating by the map origin
items.details:
`base::ConfineRect(rect, clip_width, clip_height)` in `src/base/clip.h` confines to a window at (0, 0). All eight callers have a window that starts at the map origin, so each subtracts the origin before the call and adds it back after: three in `src/ra/map/display.cc`, one in `src/ra/map/radar.cc`, and the same four in `src/td/map/`.

Change the signature to `ConfineRect(const Rect& rect, const Rect& bounds)` and call it with `{MapCellX, MapCellY, MapCellWidth, MapCellHeight}` in the caller's unit (leptons or cells). That removes 16 subtract/add pairs. Keep the returned `ConfinedRect` and the rule for `bounded` as they are: six callers ignore `bounded`, but `Scroll_Map` in both games reads it, including for a rectangle larger than the window that does not move.

Update `src/base/clip_test.cc` with a window that is not at the origin.

items.details:
Since `ClipRect()` became a plain intersection, nothing in `src/base/clip.h` uses `OutCode` or `OutCodeOf()`. Their only users are the scaled blit (`PixelView::ScaleLocked`) and the line clipper in `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.cc`.

Move the enum, its `kIsFlagEnum` specialization and the function into that file's anonymous namespace, move the four `OutCodeTest` cases from `src/base/clip_test.cc` to a test that can reach them (or drop them if the line and scale tests in `engine_gfx_test` already cover every edge), and drop `base/attributes.h`, `base/flags.h` and `<cstdint>` from `clip.h` if nothing else there needs them. The paragraph in `ClipRect()`'s comment that names `OutCodeOf()` and `PixelView::ScaleLocked` goes with it.

Optional second step: `ScaleLocked` could intersect and compare edges too, which would leave outcodes to the line clipper alone.

items.resolution: `OutCode` and `OutCodeOf()` are now in the anonymous namespace of `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.cc`, and `clip.h` lost them along with `base/attributes.h`, `base/flags.h` and `<cstdint>`. The four `OutCodeTest` cases are replaced by three `DrawLineTest` cases in `pixel_buffer_test.cc` that clip a line at each edge from either end, which the line clipper had no test for. items.title: Define base::Any() in flags.h, next to the flag enum operators
items.details:
`src/base/flags.h` documents `base::Any(flags & ...)` as the way to test a flag enum, but the function is defined in `src/base/numeric.h`, which also pulls in `absl/log/check.h` (about 131,000 preprocessed lines). A header that only tests flags has to include both.

Move `Any()` to `flags.h`. Then every `.cc` that calls `base::Any` needs `base/flags.h` among its includes (`misc-include-cleaner` enforces it) and may lose `base/numeric.h` if it used nothing else from it; count the call sites first, since this is a tree-wide include change.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: Moved `base::Any()` from `base/numeric.h` to `base/flags.h` and its test to `flags_test.cc`. Of the 28 callers outside `src/base`, 22 gained `base/flags.h` and 10 that used nothing else from it lost `base/numeric.h`; two plan docs name the new header.

items.title: Give base::Point an operator== and compare whole ConfinedRects in the clip test
items.details:
`base::Point` (`src/base/point.h`) has no `operator==`, although `base::Rect` has a defaulted one. `ExpectConfined()` in `src/base/clip_test.cc` therefore compares `position.x`, `position.y` and `bounded` one by one, and a failure reports the helper's line rather than the test's.

Add `friend constexpr bool operator==(const Point&, const Point&) = default;` to `Point` and the same to `ConfinedRect` in `src/base/clip.h`, then write the tests as `EXPECT_EQ(ConfineRect(...), (ConfinedRect{{x, y}, bounded}))` and delete the helper. Add a `PrintTo()` or `operator<<` for the two types in the test, or gtest prints a failed comparison as a byte dump. Check first that neither game defines its own comparison of points, which would become ambiguous.
items.author: agent
items.resolution: `base::Point` and `base::ConfinedRect` have a defaulted `operator==`, and `ConfinedRect` a hidden-friend `PrintTo()` like `PaletteIndex` has, so a failed comparison shows `{(x, y), bounded}`. The `ConfineRect` tests compare whole `ConfinedRect` values and `ExpectConfined()` is gone. `Point` got no printer, to keep `<ostream>` out of `point.h`; neither game defined a comparison of its own.

items.title: Test the diagonal line clipping and the scaled blit's right and bottom clipping
items.details:
`tools/coverage.py src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.cc --tests engine_gfx` shows two clipping paths in `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer.cc` that no test reaches:

- `PixelView::DrawLineLocked`: the `DrawLineTest` cases in `src/engine/gfx/pixel_buffer_test.cc` only clip horizontal and vertical lines, so the slope arithmetic that moves the other coordinate when an end is cut (`y1 += -x1 * (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)` and its seven siblings) always adds zero. Most of the diagonal stepping after the clip is unreached as well. Add diagonal lines that cross each edge, one that crosses a corner (two bits set in one outcode), and check the pixels.
- `PixelView::ScaleLocked`: `ScaleTest.ClipsRowsOffTheTopOfTheDestination` is the only clipping test. The branches for a source that runs past the right or bottom of its view, and for a destination that runs past the right or bottom of `dest`, are unreached. Add a case for each, with and without scaling, since each clipped edge moves the other rectangle by a scaled amount.

Tests only; if one shows wrong pixels, file the bug rather than change the expectation.
